title: Separable ODEs, equilibrium solutions, and maximal intervals
terms: separable equation; separation of variables; equilibrium solution; constant solution; maxi- mal interval; finite-time blow-up.

exposition.text:
′
An equation y = f(x)g(y) is separable: where g(y) ̸= 0, write dy/g(y) = f(x) dx and integrate
both sides. A solution can remain implicit. If g(c) = 0, the constant function y = c is an
equilibrium solution, which division by g(y) would remove. Check these solutions separately.
R
Antiderivatives involving logarithms require absolute values, such as dy/y = log |y| + C.
After solving, choose the branch and the maximal interval containing the initial point on which
the original equation and solution are defined. A finite denominator zero can cause blow-up.
y
Conversely, if integration yields e = H(x), then H(x) > 0 is essential; y = log |H(x)| would
incorrectly add a branch.

(A) y = log(1 − x) on (−∞, 1) (B) y = log |1 − x| on R \ {1}
(C) y = − log(1 − x) on (−∞, 1) (D) y = log(1 + x) on (−1, ∞)

Multiply by e and integrate: (e ) = −1, so e = 1 − x. Positivity of the exponential forces
x < 1 and the solution is log(1 − x). An absolute value would add an invalid branch for x >
1, and a disconnected set would not be a maximal solution interval through zero.

question.text:
′ 2
What are all constant solutions of y = y (y − 2)(y + 1)?
(A) Every constant (B) y = −1, 2 only
(C) y = 0 only (D) y = −1, 0, 2
(E) y = 0, 2 only

solution.text:
A constant solution has derivative zero, so its value must be a root of the right side. The
distinct roots are −1, 0, 2; the repeated factor at zero contributes only one constant solu-
tion.
